header.title: Physiognomonica (epitome Matritensis): AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Adamantius Judaeus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tlg0731.tlg003.1st1K-grc1, from Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0731.tlg003.1st1K-gr: The stretch begins mid-sentence; the stray 'ν' before μεγάλοι is taken as a scanning or apparatus mark. The marginal 'Matr.' markers are edition notes and are omitted. Scanning errors read as evident: πεποικιλμένοι, ξηροί (ζηροί), ἰσχυρούς, ἀνόμους, ἀχλυώδεις (ἀγλυώδεις). κέγχροι, literally 'millet grains', denotes speckles in the iris; ἴτυς ('rim, ring') is taken as a coloured ring of the iris. χαροποί is uncertain in sense (bright-eyed or light-eyed, possibly tawny). In 1.10.1 the syntax is loose and 'their thought' is a rendering of an awkward phrase.

1.11: text breaks off (lacuna). 1.13: lacunae; πισταί is a fragment, untranslatable. 2.25: 'not the character of a vulture' (γυπός) is odd and possibly corrupt; 'hard hair is good, for it is a sign of wildness' also seems corrupt or contradictory. Lacuna after 'beasts'. 2.26: lacunae in the gait section; the singular 'signifies' after a plural subject is in the text. 2.20: 'thin... shrivelled' presumably refers to knees or legs. Read προκείμεναι, κνῆμαι, κόμη, δακτύλους, κουφόνουν for scanning errors.

Marginal 'Matr.' markers omitted. 2.27: πανοῦργος glossed 'knavish'; μωροπόνηροι rendered 'knavish fools'. 2.28: ἀτρενμές read as ἀτρεμές; ὑποβρύχῃ uncertain ('rumbles below'). 2.29: γαστρίνμαργον, αὐχνμηρόν and φεγγόμενοι read as γαστρίμαργον, αὐχμηρόν and φθεγγόμενοι. 2.30: ἦμοι read as ὦμοι; 'μέτωπον τέλειον οὐ μήν τε ὀλίγον' is obscure and possibly corrupt. 2.37: ὑπέρινοι is unclear and possibly corrupt; left untranslated. 2.38: 'χειρῶν φέρεται ὡς ἀνάταυρος' is obscure, and ἀνάταυρος was not identified. 2.39: the bracketed [φορεῖν] is treated as deleted. 2.40: κίνημα σκολιόν ('curving movement') is odd in context. 2.41: βλέιμμα read as βλέμμα. Lacunae in 2.28, 2.29, 2.43 and 2.44 are kept as dots.

nodes.text: … the pupils, and large eyes that glitter, moving and staring with passion, whose lids open wide: these are useless for everything. For these are the forms of wolves and wild boars. And [the eye] gleams within like fire; and besides this, pale yellow *kenchroi* (millet-grain speckles) are mixed with fiery ones, and others are grey-blue. In short, as was said above, those who have the signs of wolves and wild boars are crueller, wilder and more rapacious. But when [the speckles] are larger or smaller, they indicate gentler [natures]. Blood-red speckles in black eyes reveal poisoners, just as pale yellow ones show men skilled in sorcery and drug-craft. The pale yellow are more deceitful, the blood-red more thoughtless and rash in action. As for those who are bright-eyed not through speckles but are variegated, examine the size and colour of these. If a black or a reddish [ring] appears in moist eyes, and nothing else odd shows, they indicate a man high-minded, just, intelligent, well-endowed by nature, but a lover of boys beyond measure; but if a greenish ring [lies] on black [eyes], [they indicate a man] deceitful, unjust, a thief, consorting with women shamefully and strangely. Rings of varied colour, like rainbows, in rather dry eyes signify vanity, but in moist ones high-mindedness and courage and straight speech and right counsel; but [such men are] quicker to anger and excitable in sexual matters.

Very hollow eyes are not praiseworthy; but those that, while hollow, are like water in a vessel and do not move about, being large, are not wicked, unless some other sign makes them so. For moisture and size soften the hollowness. The characters of the hollow and small are deceitful, treacherous among men, wasted by jealousy and envy; and of the rather dry, in addition to the evils mentioned, they signify faithlessness, treachery, temple-robbery and things like these. Those that stare fixedly display more extreme characters, those that drift more deceitful ones; but if they drift with dimness, they signify more foolish ones.

Of protruding eyes, which are not praiseworthy, some have a swelling around them in a circle, while around others runs something like a deep and narrow trench: a deceitful character. Those that stand out altogether denote profligacy, vanity and madness. The bulging of bloodshot eyes is a sign of drunkards and gluttons. If the same eyes are grey-blue, understand [such men] to be unjust and unintelligent; and if their lids are heavy, the folly is greater. If they are swollen and dry, [they are] parricides and matricides and child-murderers and poisoners and the like. But if the eyes are prominent, large, bright, clear and moist in their look, [they are] just, intelligent, eager to learn, full of love, such as was the philosopher Socrates. Eyes that protrude far from the face, very small and reddish, declare the man to be not only witless but also slack in tongue and body.

Small, quivering eyes expose men as ill-scheming and deceitful, large ones as senseless and vain. Those that quiver as though leaping out also signify bad men, unless they are of a good size and look moist and bright; for such eyes indicate an intelligent man, accomplishing energetic, lofty and great deeds, reaching the height of daring and high-mindedness, but [men] without control of anger and drink, boastful, light-minded, not far from epilepsy, who think they have glory greater than befits men, like Alexander of Macedon. Puffy eyes [indicate men who are] unstable, savage in temper, gluttonous, lustful, lyre-players, pipe-players, musicians; and [eyes] that also have the signs from within, they say, show the men to be such. Livid-rimmed eyes, if they also have the signs within, declare such men faithless, unjust and capable of any outrage.

Dark eyes signify men of little wit; being dry, they indicate more lawless men, and if they are also small and murky, [men who are] treacherous, given to evil arts, scheming. Dark, moist, hollow eyes of sufficient size indicate a steady, thoughtful man, who observes much, learns well, is cautious, timid and sparing; but dull-sighted ones [indicate men who are] deceitful, faithless, licentious.
Bright, clear eyes are the best, unless some other sign speaks against them; for one must examine all the signs carefully.

If the eyes flash alike, even if there is light in them, they are not good. For if flashing is found in grey-blue and bloodshot eyes, it indicates one hot in anger, and in every matter a hot man, capable of any outrage and close to madness; but if it is in bright-eyed ones, it signifies cowardice, for these fear everything, fall [into panic] and suspect everything. Black eyes that flash are the worst, cowardly and very ill-scheming, and they indicate the men to be such. Those who have such eyes and are given to laughter, that is, laughing slyly, reach the extreme of all wickedness. Eyes with a fierce, moist look signify such men as passionate, strong, frenzied, quick of speech, quick of action, improvident, but lacking boldness in speaking, and bad. Dry eyes signify the worst and most lawless men, and smaller, hollow ones worse: [men] savage in temper, treacherous, secretive, that is, hiding their aims and secretly robbing others. If with such eyes they have a brow that bends down with rough eyebrows, and have straight lids, it signifies spirit, strength, thoughtlessness, guilelessness and boldness. But those who do not have the brow, the lids and the eyebrows so, but whose look is in itself bitter and harsh, are worse than those mentioned before.

Eyes in which pleasure and laughter dwell are praiseworthy, but not wholly; for among these too there are deceitful men who hide their mind and their aims, ill-scheming, villainous. Those who look askance while laughing and are dry indicate the worst men.

Hollow eyes that laugh are plotting some evil, as if lying in ambush. If the parts outside the eyes, the forehead, cheeks, eyebrows and lip, move [with it], this laughter is bad, straining to arrive at a wicked and unjust plan. And if, besides this grin, they half-close and look fixedly, they are planning unjust deeds; but if they have the eyes open and grinning, that is, stretched wide, their actions move towards lawless deeds. Divine that eyes which laugh greatly are more treacherous; but if they are rather dry, [the characters are] guileless but vain, untouched by evils, and such men are without affection and licentious. Smiling eyes together with moisture, relaxed lids, a soft forehead, and loose skin around the lids indicate characters that are magnificent, just, gentle, pious, hospitable, intelligent, of good counsel, quick to learn, and full of love.

Eyes that scowl, that is, look gloomy, together with moisture, bear witness to a thoughtful man or one devoted to his craft; and if they half-close and the eyebrows slacken and the forehead appears relaxed along with the scowl, their characters are faithful and steadfast, of good counsel and self-controlled. Dry eyes with a sorrowful look are full of friendliness. If the forehead is also rough, the look fixed and the lids straight, they signify a man of savage purpose.

Eyes that shut and open again signify a treacherous and thievish man, but if they are moist, a thoughtful man devoted to his craft. If there is trembling in them together with pallor, it signifies madness and indicates epilepsy in the man. As for eyes that are always still: if, as they close, they drift and move upwards, they indicate licentiousness, that is, a profligate man, and denote one vain and raving; but if they close while upright and are moist, with size, brightness and a smooth forehead, they signify such a man as cautious, of good counsel, eager to learn, sweet-minded and amorous; but if they are dry, a bold, ill-scheming and unjust man. If besides this one has a rough forehead, drawn-together eyebrows, and hard, fixed lids, such a man appears wilder in spirit, readier to dare, yet puffed up by praise and honours and persuaded by gifts. Those who do not have straight lids or unbending eyebrows, but have trembling in them, and whose look moves about at the same time, are effeminate men who force themselves to be men.

Eyes that open wide and at the same time stand still as though thinking something signify of what kind their thought is; as has been said, it is indicated by the dry, the moist, the dark, the bright, small and large, hollow, prominent, soft, fixed, and the other qualities beyond these, which have often been discussed.

So eyes that are always open, being dark and moist, [signify] thoughtful men, and if besides this they look gently, they signify good men too. Eyes spread wide open, dry, flashing, with a clear and bright look, indicate shameless men capable of any outrage.

Blinking eyes are accusers of cowardice; for such people are also divined to be treacherous, or to be secretly preparing some evil. These same eyes, if distorted or somewhat pale, indicate foolishness. Unblinking eyes with a terrible look are contriving some evil. But [eyes] standing gently still, with moisture in them, signify men who are thoughtful, eager to learn, possessed of gentle characters and amorous. Those which, being unblinking, appear pale or crimson together with dryness reveal wickedness and strife, or anger, or demonic evil . . . . . .
Bags under the eyes, projecting below, indicate drunken, sleepy men.

Sharp, agitated eyes signify rapacious men; but if, being thin, they drop the lids over [them], they signify an effeminate man. If they lower one of the lids ... . . [...], such men are adulterers. If others close and draw down the middle of the lids, but raise both ends . . . ., they too are adulterers; likewise also those who raise the middle of the lids but close both ends.

Eunuchs who are so by nature have the same signs of wickedness as other people, and for the most part they are savage-minded, deceitful and malicious, some more than others. In the case of 〈castrated〉 eunuchs, the signs change along with the castration, but the greater part of the inborn nature remains.

Broad, white, yellowish nails indicate well-endowed men; narrow, elongated and curved ones, insensitive and bestial men; crooked ones, extremely rapacious men; those grown far into the flesh, rapacious, insensitive and bestial men. Very small nails are a sign of knavery; likewise also pale, black and rough ones. Very round ones are a sign of adulterers. However, as was said before, most of the other [signs] too are not worth much if one examines each one by itself alone, and nails above all.

Those who have fused fingers are swinish, that is, piggish, and foul; those who have them drawn together are knavish, malicious, money-loving. When they are very small and thin, they indicate rather foolish men. Thick, stubby fingers indicate a daring, improvident and bestial man; and very long and thin ones signify men rather foolish, rather vain, rather given to babble; but those who have well-sized and well-formed fingers are the best men.

Sinewy, well-jointed feet signify a man's noble character and courage; but tender and rather fleshy feet produce characters of the same kind, that is, tender, and signify such men as giving way in everything. Stubby, thick feet are indicative of a bestial soul; very long ones belong to a meddlesome or ill-scheming man; small, thin feet signify that their owner is a knave. Arched feet, or those hollow underneath, are bad; likewise those who have the underside flat and walk as if on their ankles indicate that their owners are knaves.

Well-defined, firm ankles announce a noble man; soft and smooth ones, a rather unmanly one; very thin ones are signs of a deceitful and licentious man. Thick ankles, rough heels, fleshy feet, stubby toes and thick shins make men mostly crazed or possessed by a demon.

Well-sized, well-jointed, firm shins signify noble and well-endowed men; tender and unjointed ones indicate that the man is rather cowardly and unmanly; very thin ones indicate a 〈cowardly and〉 malicious man; those that are sinewy besides indicate one given to much licentiousness. Shins that are full, being thick towards the middle, signify loathsome, profligate and shameless men; and for the most part thickness of the shins and heels indicates a servile and ignorant man. Say the same of the thighs as of the shins.
Those whose knees bend inward so as to knock together are womanish; thin, scantily fleshed, shrivelled [knees], as if wasted away, indicate a knavish man; for such too are 〈those〉 of apes.

As is clear from what was said before, black colouring signifies that the man has 〈cowardice〉 and much scheming; white and yellowish colouring speaks of strength and spirit; very white, unmixed colouring tends to unmanliness; a body red all over signifies the man's deceitfulness and versatility. A sallow, greenish complexion indicates cowardice together with ill-scheming, unless it has come from illness. The colour called honey-pale is cowardly, gluttonous, talkative, irascible, wagging the tongue; the flame-like colour is frenzied; the gently red is well-endowed, quick to learn, quick-moving.
This is about the whole body; but part by part, a reddish chest announces that anger is boiling within, just as one must examine the veins of the neck and those in the temples.
Faces red in colour of themselves indicate harsh men; but if only the cheeks are such, consider the men to be drunkards.

About the colours in the eyes something was said earlier, but what need requires will also be said here. Eyes that are reddish, if with dryness, indicate irascible people; if with moistness, they signify drunkards. Grey-blueness in the eyes says the man is rather wild; for most wild animals are grey-blue[-eyed], whereas you will find the tame ones somehow black-eyed. Of grey-blue eyes, the very white kind indicates a cowardly man, the bilious kind a wild man; the kind like olives in colour signifies a powerful man. Of the black, the very black kind indicates a cowardly and deceitful man, the yellowish kind a strong and great-souled man. Flashing eyes indicate vain men; pale eyes with varied colours signify such a man as rejoicing and suspected of thieving; glittering eyes indicate lustful and cowardly men.

Say without any dispute that a very curly-haired man is cowardly and greedy for gain, and a straight-haired one rather wild and rather foolish. The best hair is that which holds the mean between these. Extreme thickness of hair signifies a bestial man; for so it is with beasts too . . . . . . . . ; the mean in hair is praiseworthy. To be covered with very soft hair is womanish; yet they do not have the character of a vulture. Hard hair is good; for such is a sign of wildness. Black hair indicates cowardice and great greed for gain; very blond and whitish hair, such as that of the Scythians and Celts, displays ignorance, clumsiness and wildness; but the gently yellowish tends to aptness for learning, gentleness and good fortune. Unmixed redness, like the pomegranate's flower, is a sign of men who are not good; for their characters are for the most part bestial. Legs covered with very thick and long hair signify slowness to learn and wildness; those whose loins and thighs, apart from the other parts, are very hairy, these men are lustful 〈and〉 adulterers. When you see a belly and chest with much hair, say such a man is light-minded, fickle and lewd. A chest by itself covered with shaggy hair signifies hot-tempered, stout-hearted men. Hair on the shoulders and upper back indicates men like birds in their souls; for their thoughts are shown to be lofty and their plans steadfast. The whole body thickly hairy indicates the man is ox-like in his thoughts. When the neck is shaggy near the head, take the man to be powerful and stout-hearted. And when the forehead advances in the middle and the hair recedes on each side, it shows [a man] full of greatness of soul and power. Hair standing upright accuses the man of cowardice and ill-scheming. Those whose eyebrows bend down towards the nose, while on each side they go towards the temples, liken to pigs; for they are such in mind and soul. Those with eyebrows strongly joined are gloomy; for grief suits them.

Those who take long strides are accomplishers of every matter, great-minded; those who take small strides are ineffective, bitter and ... ... ... plotting secretly; quick-moving ones, together with uprightness and brightness of appearance, signify a hot-tempered man, an undertaker [of things], not a doer. .... .... Together with quick movement, agitation in the eyes, unsteadiness of the head and panting are the marks of a man who does evil, has great ambitions, and is to be shunned. He who walks quickly but with small steps is greedy for gain, malicious, full of cowardice to the utmost. A leisurely gait, if natural, signifies the man as rather sluggish and deep-minded, but gentle, unless the weightier signs contradict it. But if he slows down deliberately, and stops in the streets and looks around, it indicates their haughty characters, and [that they are] insolent, arrogant and adulterous.

It is good to have the hands and feet alike in every way in carriage and movement. He who moves slightly at the shoulders and is at the same time gently stooped has a fair share of great-mindedness and courage. He who moves slightly at the shoulders, but is upright and holds his neck high, is disobedient, self-willed and insolent; for a horse too walks in the same way. And you could infer the rest likewise from these. Those who move with the whole body at once and with each of the limbs separately are effeminate. For this is plainly womanish. Effeminate too are those who lean to the right as they move. Those who lean away to the left are more foolish. Those who bend themselves down, stooping, are flatterers.

Breath that is always still, so that it seems [he is] breathless, belongs to a thoughtful man. Of what sort the thought is, one must learn precisely from the eyes and not leave unknown. But if, after being still for a long time, it appears all at once in one who is speaking, like an ebb and a flood tide, he is gripped by some grief. If he moves his head and at the same time sighs, he seems to repent of having done or seen something bad. If [he does so] with staring eyes, he is planning these evils beforehand rather than repenting. Breath that goes slowly and passes without noise indicates a mind in good order. But when it rumbles below and he breathes heavily, it accuses wildness and drunkenness. The asthmatic, whose breath is driven as if from running, are thoughtless, ill-tempered . . . . babblers. Those who breathe through the nostrils are cowardly and despondent; they also prove effeminate when the other signs bear witness with these.

To speak very deep and cracked indicates a foolish and insolent man, and a glutton. A rather ill-sounding and bleating sound indicates an insensible man. Those whose voice begins deep and ends high, such men are complainers and despondent. To speak high and grating is the sign of a wily man, if [it is] high and harsh. But if he speaks high, soft 〈and〉 supple, it signals such a man to be effeminate. Those who sound hollow, deep and unbending have noble characters, and think highly of them. Those who speak soft and deep, count their thoughts good too. Those who speak shrilly, that is, shouting high and bird-like, think vain, empty and lofty things. A weak voice that is at the same time tearful signifies a man greedy for gain, grating, and suspected in everything. Those who speak through the nose are false, malicious and envious, rejoicing in the harm of others, and simply dangerous. To speak violently 〈and〉 somewhat cracked indicates anger and violence 〈and lawlessness〉 and misanthropy. To speak high and weak is a sign of cowardice and malice in the man; to speak briefly is a sign of idleness and cowardice; [to speak] fast 〈indicates〉 a rash and foolish man. Those who speak with difficulty are shown for the most part to be bad and foolish. But if anything else ....................................

The courageous type: the whole bearing upright, the sides and all the joints of the body strong, bones large, hair stiff, belly broad and hollow, shoulders strong, shoulder-blades wide and set apart, chest and upper back robust, hips firm, legs fleshy, strength about the ankles, feet well-jointed, colour rather sharp, gaze moist, eyes not large, nor again wide open, nor yet closed, eyebrows not stretched, forehead full, yet not small, voice rather harsh, strong, loud, breath steady. Such is the stout-hearted and strong man.

The signs of the cowardly type are these: soft hair, the whole bearing slack, a long neck, honey-coloured complexion, agitated eyes, quick-moving eyelids, panting in breath, thin legs, long loins, weak chest, long hands, a shrill soft voice.

The signs of the well-endowed are these: of good size, being white and reddish, with hair not very curly nor straight, the whole body upright, the joints loosely set from one another, flesh moderate and tender, legs and thighs well-nourished, ankles strong, the joints of feet and hands well-made, fingers tender, of good length, set apart from one another, the face raised and fleshy, yet not thin, eyes moist, bright, bright-eyed, the 〈character〉 in them joyful.

These are the signs of the insensible: very white or very black, fleshy or pot-bellied, thick-legged, with joints small and bound together, having collar-bones grown together and a stunted, thick neck, imperfect extremities, fleshy cheeks, a round forehead, a dull, gaping gaze.

34. The signs of a shameless man are these: eyes wide open and bright, eyelids spread open and thick, thick-footed, thick-nosed, looking straight at [one], stretching himself upward, ruddy in colour, high in voice.
The orderly man speaks deep, but briefly, and he moves his eyelids moderately, neither continually nor at long intervals; he is bright-eyed, looking not brightly but moistly, and full of blushes.

Signs of the cheerful man: forehead fleshy, smooth, low, and the whole face rather fleshy, the appearance sleepy, eyes bright, not staring, movement leisurely, voice gentle. Such are the signs of the cheerful man.
These are the signs of the gloomy man: a lean face, eyebrows drawn in, eyelids tensed; he moves as though *hyperinoi*.

These are the signs of the effeminate: he looks moist and bold, and his eyes quiver and run about; he contracts his forehead and cheeks; his eyebrows do 〈not〉 stay in place; his neck is bent; his loins are not still; all his limbs move, and he is jumpy, knock-kneed; he carries his hands like an *anatauros*; he glances at himself and looks around; his voice is thin, screeching, shrill, very slow, and trembling.
A bitter man [is given] to grinning, looking harsh and dry, having a wrinkled forehead, speaking violently, panting, and clapping or rubbing his hands, often stamping his feet.

The gentle man is by nature strong in his whole body, well-fleshed, his flesh moist and soft, well-proportioned in his limbs, his gaze steady, his movement short and curving, his voice deep and soft, the line of his hair springing upward.
The dissembler and contrarian has slack eyes, a somewhat dainty gaze, a lowered voice; he walks with easy turns and moves everything rhythmically.
〈Take〉 the money-loving man to be such: small-limbed, small-eyed, small-faced, quick in walking, stooping, quick-voiced, high-voiced, reddish in colour.
A man shaggy with hair, straight-bearded or black, having a shaggy moustache, temples ........ flashing, fond of revelling, fond of dancing, fond of wine. These are the signs of the two types.

There are also knavish fools, who have mixed signs of knavery and folly. Others have the same signs of folly and have been made harsher and wilder. From this, then, there are knavish fools, just as among beasts of the same kind some are tame and others wild, ....... more simple ... and more agitated for the most part. This you could observe especially in wild goats and sheep, and further in horses and asses and all such; though alike in form, the tame are gentler and smoother, ........ and so their characters follow their forms. And among humans, then, one must distinguish in this way; for this twofold form appears in humans in each sign. For just men arise from the same signs. But some have wilder characters, others tamer, and likewise the temperate and the courageous. The difference of the signs must be distinguished by roughness and smoothness, hardness and softness, agitation and gentleness, and by moist and dry. So it is also with injustice and licentiousness; for in these signs too, though they are the same, the tameness or wildness that grows with them shows the one injustice as wilder, the other as milder; and among the effeminate, most are wild, but others are tame. And since there are no other signs for these, they are distinguished only by those I have mentioned.
